paragraphs.heading: Calculus for random paths
paragraphs.text: Itô calculus is a way of doing calculus with quantities that move at random. Named after Kiyosi Itô, it carries the methods of calculus over to stochastic processes, that is, random processes, such as Brownian motion. Its central tool is the Itô stochastic integral, a random version of the Riemann–Stieltjes integral from analysis. Integrating in this way gives back another stochastic process: for any fixed end time t, the integral from 0 to t is a random variable, defined as the limit of a sequence of random variables.

paragraphs.heading: Why ordinary calculus fails
paragraphs.text: The usual techniques of calculus cannot be applied to the paths of Brownian motion, because those paths do not meet the conditions the techniques need. Such a path has no derivative at any point. Over every stretch of time, its total up-and-down movement, called its variation, is infinite. So when the thing being integrated is random, the Itô integral has to be taken against a function of exactly this rough kind.

paragraphs.heading: Building the integral
paragraphs.text: The key insight is that the integral can still be defined as long as the integrand, written H, is adapted. Loosely, that means its value at time t may use only information available up to time t. To build the integral, one cuts the interval from 0 to t into a sequence of ever finer pieces and forms Riemann sums over them, taking the limit in probability as the pieces shrink to nothing. Which point inside each small piece is used to evaluate the function matters a great deal, and the usual choice is the left end. Showing that this limit exists, and that it does not depend on the chosen sequence of pieces, takes many technical details.

paragraphs.heading: Its own rules
paragraphs.text: Itô calculus has its own versions of familiar rules, including an integration by parts formula and Itô's lemma, a change of variables formula. These differ from the formulas of ordinary calculus because of extra quadratic variation terms. An alternative, the Stratonovich integral, does follow the ordinary chain rule and needs no Itô's lemma. It uses the average of the random quantity over each small time step, while the Itô integral looks only at the start of the step. The two forms can be converted into each other.

paragraphs.heading: A trading example
paragraphs.text: In finance, the way the Itô integral is evaluated is pictured as deciding first what to do and only then watching the prices change. Stock prices can be modelled by Brownian motion or, more commonly, by geometric Brownian motion. Think of the integrand as how much stock you hold, the integrator as the movement of prices, and the integral as your total money, including what your stock is worth, at each moment. The Itô integral is then the payoff of a trading strategy that holds an amount Hₜ of stock at time t. Requiring H to be adapted means the strategy can use only what is known at the time, which rules out unlimited gains from seeing the future, such as buying just before every rise and selling just before every fall.

paragraphs.heading: Shorthand and uses
paragraphs.text: The integral is often written in differential form as dY = H dX, which means the same as Y − Y₀ = H · X. The adapted condition also has a technical payoff: it keeps the integral from diverging when it is computed as a limit of Riemann sums. The calculus has important uses in mathematical finance and stochastic differential equations, and more recently in machine learning.
